format.limits: This statement covers only records counter-signed on this chain at ledger seq from..to, and the attachment entries it lists. Records never submitted to this ledger are outside it, and nothing here says the issuer issued no other records. An attachment entry names the position of a record on this chain at or before seq to; Tersign lists entries and does not verify them. Binding declared: the attachment is the record at that position, bound by the counter-signed link at that position. Binding sealed: the attachment is sealed inside the v2 chain link at that position. Issuer-sequence gaps and duplicates are reported only for records whose counter-signed link binds the issuer seq, only between the lowest and highest such seq in the range, and only against records counter-signed at or before seq to; an omission after the highest bound seq is not detectable. It restates the ledger's contemporaneous counter-signatures and the anchor named, and its own signature adds no earlier time. It is not a statement about record content, tax treatment or compliance with any law.

parse.rule: The served body is JSON text; no object carries a member name twice; every number token is an integer in [-(2**53 - 1), 2**53 - 1] (a fraction or exponent token is not, even when its value is an integer); every string, member names included, is well-formed Unicode (a surrogate that is not half of a pair has no UTF-8 form). Otherwise parse. A body that is JSON text but not an object is refused by the envelope rule, as shape.

raw_surrogate.rule: The text is read as code points. A surrogate code point written raw in the text, not as a \u escape, is refused, even where an escaped surrogate next to it would complete a pair, so either half of a pair written raw is refused; a character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane written raw is one code point, not a surrogate, and is accepted. Otherwise parse. The format's parse rule does not say whether the text is read as code points or as UTF-16 code units; JSON.parse, a reader of UTF-16 code units, joins the two halves into a pair. A body served as UTF-8 cannot carry a raw surrogate, so the rule changes no verdict on a served body; this suite fixes it so that a reader of code points and a reader of UTF-16 code units agree.

byte_order_mark.rule: A byte-order mark (U+FEFF) before the JSON value is refused: it is not JSON whitespace (RFC 8259 section 2). Otherwise parse. RFC 8259 section 8.1 forbids adding one to a JSON text sent over a network and lets a parser ignore one; this suite refuses it, as JavaScript's JSON.parse and Python's json.loads over text do, so that conformant engines give one answer for one text. Whether a decoder removes the mark from served bytes before the text reaches an engine is outside the profile. A ledger that follows section 8.1 serves no mark, so the rule changes no verdict on such a body; it decides text a verifier is handed.

depth.rule: The body nests objects and arrays at most format.max_depth deep, the body object counting 1, counted on the text. Otherwise parse. The format sets no bound; this suite fixes one so that where a body nested past it is refused does not depend on where a parser stops, which differs between parsers and interpreters. At or below the bound the body is still parsed, and statement/verify_statement.py parses with json.loads, which recurses: a caller near its interpreter's recursion limit can get parse there for a body the other engine reads. So the two engines agree on every vector, not for every caller. A statement nests 8 deep at most, so the bound changes a reason, never a verdict. The vectors sit at the bound and at 3,000 levels, not between.

envelope.rule: The body is an object with exactly the members {statement, statementDigest, signature, signer} (a body that is JSON text but not an object, an array for example, is refused here), and signer equals statement.ledger byte for byte. Otherwise shape.

members.rule: The statement's members are exactly the fourteen in format.statement_members; schema, limits and commitmentSchema are the fixed values in format, compared byte for byte; ledger is 0x + 40 hex digits in either letter case. Otherwise shape.

scope.rule: scope is a member whose value is one of format.scopes, compared exactly. A value outside the set, null and the empty string reject as scope; a statement without the member rejects as shape.

chain.rule: chain is {sellerId} or {sellerId, key}; sellerId is a non-empty string (shape). key, when present, is 0x + 64 lower-case hex digits other than 32 zero bytes (chain_key).

range.rule: range is exactly {from, to} (shape) of integers with 1 <= from <= to and at most format.max_range records (range).

attachments.rule: attachments is exactly {version, entries} and version is the JSON integer 1 (attachments_version); entries is an array (attachment_entry).

entries.rule: Each entry is exactly {position, type, binding}. position is an integer, 1 <= position <= range.to (it may lie before range.from), strictly ascending across entries. binding is one of format.bindings, compared exactly. Otherwise attachment_entry.

entry_type.rule: type is 2-64 characters: a lower-case letter, then lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, ending in a letter or digit; and a type made only of hex digits and hyphens that holds format.type_hex_digits or more hex digits is refused (hyphens are not counted; one character outside [0-9a-f-] takes a type outside this rule). Otherwise attachment_entry.

sealed.rule: A sealed entry needs a v2 link at its position. The first v2 link of the range is at range.from + linkVersions.v1, so when linkVersions.v1 > 0 a sealed entry at any position below it, positions before range.from included, rejects as attachment_entry. When linkVersions.v1 is 0 the statement says nothing about links before range.from, and a sealed entry there is not checked.

before_through.rule: before is {seq, head, acc}: seq an integer, head null or 0x + 64 lower-case hex, acc 0x + 64 lower-case hex; through is {seq, head, acc}: seq an integer, head and acc 0x + 64 lower-case hex (shape). before.seq = range.from - 1; before.head is null exactly when before.seq is 0; at seq 0, before.acc is the commitment seed keccak256(utf8("tersign-chain-commitment-v1")); through.seq = range.to (consistency).

link_versions.rule: linkVersions is exactly {v1, v2} of non-negative integers (shape), and v1 + v2 counts every record of the range (consistency).

issuer_seq.rule: issuerSeq is exactly {boundRecords, unboundRecords, absentRecords, listCap, series, truncated}: non-negative integers, a boolean and an array (shape). listCap is format.list_cap; unboundRecords = linkVersions.v1 and boundRecords + absentRecords = linkVersions.v2; with no bound record there is no series; series, each series' missing numbers and its duplicates are each at most listCap long; series ids ascend strictly and 0 <= min <= max; missing numbers are integers ascending strictly within [min, max]; a duplicate names at least two ledger seqs, integers strictly ascending, each from 1 to range.to (consistency). A series is exactly {series, min, max, missing, duplicates}: series 0x + 64 lower-case hex, min and max integers, missing and duplicates arrays; a duplicate is exactly {seq, correctionSeq, ledgerSeqs}: seq an integer, correctionSeq null or a non-negative integer, ledgerSeqs an array (shape).

issuer_report.rule: The report is computed from the link bindings as the format defines it: the counts, and each series' min and max, over the range; a series reported when a bound record in the range names it; a number missing when no original (correctionSeq null) binding at or before range.to names it; a duplicate a (seq, correctionSeq) named by two or more bindings at or before range.to, one of them in the range. Four consequences of that definition are checked, each otherwise consistency. After the list cap and before the first series: there are at most boundRecords series, since a record names one series. After each duplicate's ledger-seq rule: its seq lies within its series' [min, max], since one of its bindings is in the range; with correctionSeq null, its seq is not listed missing, since an original binding makes its number present; and none of its ledger seqs is named by an earlier duplicate, in its own series or another, whatever their order in the ledger, since a record binds one (series, seq, correctionSeq). Both engines check the last three in that order; all four reject as consistency, so that order is not observable through an engine that returns a reason and no detail, and no vector pins it. The four are necessary, not sufficient: a report can keep them and still be one that no bindings produce, for example one bound record and a series whose min and max differ.

anchor.rule: anchor is null (and then bridge is null) or exactly the eleven members in format.anchor_members: subjectSchema = commitmentSchema; seq an integer >= range.to; head, acc, subjectDigest and anchoredDigest 0x + 64 lower-case hex; batchRoot null or the same; status one of format.anchor_statuses; bitcoinBlockHeight null or a non-negative integer; subjectDigest = keccak256 over canonical({acc, head, schema: subjectSchema, seq}); id = "seller:" + subjectDigest; anchoredDigest = sha256 over the 32 subject-digest bytes; proofUrl a string ending /v1/anchors/<id>/proof.ots; an anchor at range.to commits through.acc and through.head. Otherwise anchor.

bridge.rule: An anchor at range.to carries bridge null. An anchor more than format.bridge_cap records past range.to carries bridge null. Otherwise bridge is exactly {from: range.to + 1, to: anchor.seq, links}, one 0x + 64 lower-case hex link per record after range.to, and the links fold through.acc to anchor.acc (acc = keccak256(acc || link), the core's chain_commitment step). Otherwise anchor.

digest.rule: statementDigest = keccak256 over the UTF-8 bytes of canonical(statement), the canonical form the core's digest_recompute pins. Otherwise digest.

signature.rule: The signature is "0x" then 130 hex digits (r || s || v), v is 27 or 28, s <= n/2, 1 <= r < n and s >= 1, decided on the bytes before recovery, and personal_sign recovery (the construction the counter-signature profile's step 7 recovers) over the UTF-8 string format.signature_prefix + statementDigest yields statement.ledger, compared case-insensitively. Otherwise signature.

expected_signer.rule: When the relying party brings the ledger's key from elsewhere (expected_signer), it equals statement.ledger, compared case-insensitively. Otherwise signer. Without it a valid verdict says only that the key named in the statement signed it.

records.rule: When the relying party brings the range's artifact digests (records, in ledger order), there is one 0x + 64 lower-case hex digest per record of the range, and folding them from before (link = keccak256(digest || prev or 32 zero bytes || uint64_be(seq)), acc = keccak256(acc || link)) ends at through.acc with through.head as the last digest. Otherwise records.

check_order.rule: The first rule broken decides the reason, in the order the runner lists (parse, envelope, statement rules in the order of statement/verify_statement.py, signer = ledger, digest, signature, expected signer, records). The order vectors (ids containing "-order-") each carry two faults, one from each of two reason groups adjacent in that order, and expect the first group's reason; each fault alone rejects with its own reason. Together they pin every adjacent pair of reason groups, each by the one pair of rules its vector breaks, at the place in the statement where its two faults sit. The order vectors from a series' shape to a duplicate's consistency put both faults in the first series or in its first duplicate, so they pin the order inside one series or one duplicate; the issuer-counts vector puts its series fault in the second series and the series-count vector (rules.issuer_report) in the first, and one more vector pins one order across two series (the first series' consistency before the second series' shape). They do not pin other pairs of rules across a boundary, any other order across two series or two duplicates, the order among rules that share a reason, or the order among the parse rules. The engines return a reason and no detail, so the order among rules that share a reason (the four rules.issuer_report rules, all consistency, for example) is not observable through them. Every other vector breaks one rule, except where its description names a second, and expects that rule's reason.

input.rule: A vector's input is {body_text, expected_signer?, records?}: the served body as text, and the two values a relying party may bring from elsewhere, read by key presence.

twin.rule: Every rejecting vector names an accepting vector of this set, its twin, and its description names what changed: one value; one logical change that moves values bound to each other (an anchor's derived members recomputed, a count with the count that must match it, a statement signed by another key); or, for the order vectors, two faults. The runner fails a set where a twin is missing or not valid.

test_key_derivation: keccak256("evidence-record-conformance crypto-profile test key v1") mod n (the counter-signature profile's test key, crypto/MANIFEST.json)
second_test_key_derivation: keccak256("evidence-record-conformance statement-profile second test key v1") mod n
test_nonce_derivation: keccak256(the private key as 32 big-endian bytes || the 32-byte message hash) mod n, per signature
vector_provenance: every entry names author and origin = {class, source}, origin.class from the core's closed set; every vector here is synthetic. No vector carries a record, key or anchor of a live ledger, and proofUrl values use the reserved host ledger.example.
